Summary: Low back pain (LBP) is a global problem, causing disability and costing billions in healthcare. Many Australians suffer from it, and spinal surgery is a common treatment, especially for older people. Surgery isn't consistent and is costly. ASPIRE aims to change this by creating a national database of spinal surgery. It brings together experts to improve surgery outcomes and to make care more transparent and effective. ASPIRE will make LBP treatment better, safer, and higher value for everyone.

Our research has shown drastic disparities in maternal care, with over many excess neonatal deaths across different models. We aim to advance implementation of a Maternity Learning Health System across community priorities, research evidence, practice evidence and implementation to deliver evidence-based, value-based prevention and care to benefit mothers and babies nationally.

Health in pregnancy and early childhood is a key determinant of health outcomes later in life. Working with community and health service partners, this research will co-design, implement and evaluate an innovative, multidisciplinary model of care for diabetes in pregnancy in remote East Arnhem Land that is scalable across the remote NT and beyond.

Summary: Perinatal depression and anxiety (PNDA) and child learning difficulties are related problems that have major health and economic impacts. Poor diet quality during pregnancy increases the risk of both. Women in rural and remote communities have limited access to dietary advice and support. The Food PRT-E (pronounced ‘party’) clinical trial will test whether an intervention delivered by midwives improves maternal mental health and child learning outcomes in rural and remote communities.

Summary: First Nations families experience a higher burden of poor perinatal outcomes and increased risk of child protection involvement than other Australians. Culturally tailored continuity with a known midwife during pregnancy, birth & postpartum improves these outcomes but very few women having a First Nations baby in Victoria can access this care. We will facilitate model implementation and evaluation across 5 services to improve outcomes and help close the gap for ≈ 1600 First Nations babies.

Summary: The Koorlangka Keniny music program aims to teach Noongar language through song and dance to caregivers and their children to support language development and health and wellbeing, support connection to culture for caregivers and their babies and support the revitalisation of Noongar language.

Summary: This project will work in partnership with Aboriginal Elders, communities and health care providers to undertake a comprehensive examination of bereavement care services for Aboriginal peoples. It aims to enhance our understanding of the experiences of Aboriginal families in bereavement care, explore the needs of health care providers in providing optimal care and, and develop an Aboriginal-specific model of perinatal loss.

This study will develop and pilot the first community-led support program aimed at optimising iron intake for pregnant First Nations women living on Gomeroi lands.

Summary: While many people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) benefit from a total joint replacement, ~15% develop severe, debilitating chronic post-surgical pain. We will conduct a randomised controlled trial so that we understand how effective this new treatment is in terms of clinical outcome and cost.

We now propose a larger-scale study to assess the implementation of the program on a broader scale and to gain a deeper understanding of its impact for people with SCI.

Summary: APAP-YCS is a project designed with young people who have survived cancer. This project will empower young survivors through a tailored physical and lifestyle activity program to aid their recovery and to assist them to integrate their new reality with the life they want. The project will also train healthcare providers to improve their ability to help young survivors, and to enhance services and education in community settings.

This study will evaluate whether a clinician supported, virtual care telehealth model of care including exercise, nutrition, education, behaviour change, and peer support can improve fatigue and quality of life in cancer survivors, and whether this approach is translatable into clinical practice and feasible for scale-up.

We propose partnering with young people and health providers to develop and assess a survivorship program tailored to young survivors’ needs. This will empower survivors by improving equitable access to comprehensive survivorship care, helping them to thrive in the long-term.

Summary: People living with HIV (PLHIV) experience an intensive period of treatment and psychosocial adjustment following diagnosis. We will establish a new multidisciplinary multi-sectoral team that will use best practice quantitative and qualitative methods to examine, for the first time, survivorship care for PLHIV in Australia.

We will identify people who are at high risk of poor outcomes after critical illness and use novel electronic methods to improve their recovery, improving the services and communication between acute care, general practice and community care services.

This Australia-wide study will test the effectiveness of a targeted, brief early intervention in young traumatised children who have survived PICU and explore the best strategies for impactful, meaningful implementation

Summary: Domestic violence and random assaults are widespread and lead to numerous detrimental consequences, such as traumatic brain injury (TBI). Pioneering this world-first initiative, we will deploy ASPIRE, an innovative web-based platform to enhance survivorship care for violence victims with TBI. By doing so, we aim to enhance both physical and psychological long-term outcomes while simultaneously reducing healthcare costs across the Australian community.

Currently, there are no toolkits or programs that have been developed with survivors to comprehensively address this issue in Australia.

This research aims to understand the cancer-related healthcare needs and preferences of people with intellectual disability, and to co-produce resources and support tools.  We also aim to improve healthcare practices by working directly with service providers, health professionals and policymakers to enhance equity in cancer survivorship.

Our prior research shows texting can help people learn to manage chronic pain. Nearly everyone has a mobile phone, texts are cheap to send, and it avoids going to a pain clinic. Our study compares texting to a best-practice pain treatment program. If texting compares well to a pain program and people like it, it can be easily made widely available.

This kit overcomes barriers rural communities face with the existing GP-centred model of heart health check care. We recruit rural participants to test the kit's feasibility, targeting people aged 45-79, and connect medium and high-risk individuals to available risk reduction programs and primary care. Success will be measured by community uptake and experiences with the proactive model.

Summary: Digital healthcare delivery models are increasingly being used in urban areas to streamline workflows, reduce costs, and optimise patient health outcomes. Enabling the implementation and adoption of a national virtual health service by using consumer-led and culturally informed frameworks will transform healthcare access for rural and remote Indigenous populations across Australia.

Summary: Our project aims to learn about the impact of long COVID in the Northern Territory (NT), focusing on First Nations people. We will evaluate the impact of long COVID on physical health conditions and immune responses. We aim to guide future research directions and policies that contribute towards creating a service focused on First Nations people affected by long COVID in the NT.

Survivors of serious injury are required to navigate a myriad of health and social services that are underpinned by complex funding mechanisms to access the care that they need to recover. The ACTION trial will test whether implementing dedicated trauma patient navigators at Australian trauma centres enhances the experience and outcomes for survivors of serious injury and their close others, potentially transforming post-discharge care of trauma patients.

Summary: Many patients with leukaemia and bone marrow failure, or who receive high dose chemotherapy for cancer, require blood stem cell transplantation. Those without a suitably matched donor are at high risk of severe complications such as graft versus host disease. Personalised haematopoietic stem cells would provide a safe, therapeutic option for these patients. We can now generate these cells in the laboratory and we will develop techniques to make sufficient cells for patient transplantation.

Portable bioartificial kidney (BAK) devices containing living human kidney cells show promise, but face challenges in establishing an optimal cell source. This project aims to generate accurate, stable, renewable, and functional kidney cells from human stem cells for future BAK development. If successful, this could transform the BAK field, improving outcomes and quality of life for CKD patients.

Summary: There is an urgent need for innovative solutions to meet transfusion needs. Cultured red blood cells (cRBCs) produced from patient-derived stem cells in vitro represent a promising alternative. However, current in vitro production methods are financially untenable for large-scale application and there has been limited progress internationally. This incubator project will establish the feasibility of a novel approach to enhance and reduce costs of cRBC production, enabling this therapy.

Summary: Heart failure costs in Australia are over $1 Billion p.a. with 50% mortality within 1 year (stage IV disease). This arises from the heart’s limited capacity for self-repair. This project builds on our team's previous work with novel stem cell derived heart muscle, enhancing the therapeutic cell product and adding to our understanding of stakeholder needs so that this innovative treatment can seamlessly transition to later stage development and clinical trials.

Summary: Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB) is a rare genetic condition that leads to extreme skin fragility and open wounds all over the body. Currently there is no cure and treatments rely on surface dressings to protect from infection and further trauma. We propose to develop a completely new approach for the management of  EB wounds using a gel containing healing promoting agents produced by stem cells to promote healing responses.  This WoundGel would transform the treatment of wounds for people with EB.

Summary: Dementia is a leading cause of death and presents a significant and growing health issue in Australia. New effective and safer medicines are needed to treat memory, thinking and mood symptoms. We aim to create innovative and reliable, human brain cell-based models. We will combine these new models with computer-guided discovery to rapidly find new drugs with the best chance of translating into real world medicines to reduce the impact of dementia on people living with dementia and their carers.

Summary: Bowel cancer represents a critical and intractable health issue in Australia and globally. This project will generate an Australian benchmark bio-resource of 200 patient tumour models for bowel cancer and workflows for high-throughput drug development to accelerate translation of emerging therapeutics into the clinic.

Here, our internationally recognised team of stem cell biologists and clinicians, will use stem cell models of the heart to evaluate the potential of new drugs that enhance heart regeneration to treat heart failure.

However, many newly diagnosed patients have an underlying cause that has never been seen before. We will implement a new 'blood in a dish' system using patient stem cells which can both "test" which disease they have, and then find which therapies might "correct" the disease. This system will allow a new generation of diagnostics and therapies for these patients with few options.

Summary: Neuronal tumours are the leading cause of death and disease related mortality in children. In this application we intend to generate new stem-cell based models of childhood neuronal tumours to uncover how genetic defects lead to cancer, and to provide new resources for identifying better treatment options to improve outcomes and decrease treatment toxicity.

Investigators: Professor Jose Polo; Doctor Rudrarup Bhattacharjee; Professor Ryan Lister; Doctor Daniel Poppe; Doctor Adrienne Sullivan
Summary: Our project focuses on understanding and finding treatments for rare brain disorders caused by problems in how our cells control gene activity. These disorders often lead to severe learning disabilities and other serious brain disorders. We will create stem cells from patients with these disorders. By turning these stem cells into brain cells, we can make “disease models” to better understand how the diseases develop and also test many potential drugs  that might help treat the disorders.

Summary: This project aims to develop a first-in-human dendritic cell (DC)-based immunotherapy to treat patients with incurable solid cancers. It will use a world-first platform to produce type 1 conventional DCs (DC1s) at scale and supercharge them with chimeric antigen receptors (CARs). The resulting CAR-DC1s will enable enhanced tumour recognition and functionality. Program of research aims to develop technology to extend the lifespan and quality of life of patients with incurable solid cancers.

Summary: Biointelect Venturer (BV), an innovative virtual Incubatorprogram designed to accelerate the development of preventative health technologies in Australia. BV will focus on supporting Australian small-to-medium enterprises (SME) with early-stage vaccines, vaccine-related technologies, and immunotherapies for infectious diseases at TRL 2 through 6, by leveraging existing infrastructure and facilities across Australia and from BV project partners and applying specialised product development expertise, upskilling and training. Our comprehensive, national approach aims to de-risk technologies and enhance their commercial and translation potential.

Summary: High risk childhood brain tumours are the leading cause of death and disease related mortality in children. In this application we intend to use new stem-cell based differentiation models to uncover the genetic drivers of childhood brain cancer to provide new resources for identifying better treatment options to improve patient outcomes.

Summary: Gliomas, including glioblastomas, are aggressive brain cancers that are difficult to treat due to their spread into healthy brain tissue. This project develops Neutron Capture Enhanced Particle Therapy (NCEPT), a new approach combining advanced drugs and precision radiation to selectively target tumour cells while protecting healthy tissue. By collaborating with leading researchers and facilities, this work aims to create a safer, more effective treatment for patients with limited options.

Summary: Preterm infants are very susceptible to serious lung infections in conjunction with their pre-existing lung diseaseoften resulting in hospitalisation. Severe lung infections also increase the baby's chance of developing wheeze, asthma and breathing problems through life. This clinical trial will test if a mouth spray (Bactek) can prevent severe early life lung infections by training the immune system of preterm infants.

Summary: HIGH-FIVE is a Phase 3 randomized trial comparing 20-39 treatments daily radiotherapy (control arm) vs 5-treatment stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT, intervention arm) for high-risk prostate cancer, with metastases free survival as the primary end point. If 5-treatment prostate SBRT is shown to be non-inferior, this will be a new standard of care radiotherapy option for high-risk prostate cancer, with huge implication on patients’ treatment convenience and public healthcare cost saving.

Summary: Migrant and refugee women from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds experience inequities in accessing fertility treatments and poorer outcomes. This mixed-method study explores the physical and psychological impact of fertility treatment for CALD women in Australia, and the barriers and facilitators to culturally responsive care. Findings will inform the co-creation of psychoeducational support resource for CALD women and recommendations for healthcare professionals.

Summary: Infertility affects 1 in 6 couples and Australia has one of the highest rates of infertility treatment globally. Advances in care are significant, however there is a plethora of misinformation, perverse commercial incentives and limited research, evidence or translation on the physical, emotional and psychological impacts of infertility treatment for prospective parents, especially in priority populations. Here we partner to identify and mitigate impacts including a novel digital intervention.

Summary: Parents need timely, evidence-based, appropriate, and equal access to help when they are concerned during pregnancy. Getting rid of barriers and empowering parents to seek help fosters healthier pregnancies. We will deliver co-designed solutions, resources and education for both parents and healthcare professionals to support help-seeking during pregnancy and promote shared understanding for culturally safe and responsive pregnancy care.

Summary: Blood tests are commonly ordered to check on the health of the liver, kidney, thyroid and so many organs. No such health test exists for the placenta. In an Aussie-wide effort stretching from the city to remote Broome (including first Nation Australians), we will validate the first placental health blood test. A test that's simple, accurate and accessible. A high risk result will save babies from stillbirth. A low risk result will offer reassurance that the placenta is healthy and baby is safe.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Professor Gavin Pereira; Ms Olga Aleshin; Doctor Diana Bond; Doctor Laura Gerhardy; Ms Haylee Hawkins; Mrs Catherine Hughes; Professor Natasha Nassar; Professor Camille Raynes-Greenow; Doctor Antonia Shand; Associate Professor Gizachew Tessema; Doctor Kingsley Wong
Summary: Building on our previous work that developed Australia’s first stillbirth prediction model, this project will create a new, comprehensive risk tool by integrating both established and novel clinical variables. Using data from local health districts, the tool will improve prediction accuracy across diverse populations and settings. This will enable earlier identification of high-risk pregnancies, allowing for timely interventions to reduce stillbirth and improve outcomes.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: Many women experience challenging symptoms during perimenopause and menopause that can affect physical and mental health and work life. This new national study will address current knowledge gaps on perimenopause and menopause and how the impacts vary for women across Australia and from diverse communities, including their healthcare service and workplace preferences. Study findings will inform improvements in healthcare and workplace support for all women going through this life transition.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: This project focuses on the risks posed by bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BPF) in food packaging, which can harm female fertility by affecting egg quality. In Australia, there are minimal regulations on bisphenol levels in food. We aim to determine safe exposure limits and raise awareness among consumers. By combining lab studies with real-world data and engaging with the public and stakeholders, we hope to inform policy changes and improve health outcomes related to unexplained female infertility.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Doctor Sandra Richardson; Doctor Adam Ewing; Doctor Michael Pankhurst; Doctor Stephanie Workman
Summary: The reasons that some women struggle to conceive are often unknown. We will examine how bits of DNA called "jumping genes" damage the genetic code of egg cells, contributing to female infertility. We will measure jumping gene damage in young versus aging egg cells and in egg cells produced during fertility treatments. Our Research aims to explain a significant portion of female infertility cases, and lead to new strategies for improved outcomes for women experiencing infertility.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: Early pregnancy loss is common and improved care and prevention is needed. Preconception planning and treatment interventions for both intending parents are limited by poor understanding of the underlying causes. This study will investigate the importance of the female immune response, and the role of metabolic, hormone, and male partner factors to pregnancy outcome. The results are expected to provide valuable insight into causes of pregnancy loss, and will assist development of better care.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Doctor Matilda Jackson; Professor Cedric Bardy; Professor Christopher Barnett; Doctor Thi Thuong Ha; Professor Natasha Harvey; Doctor Lachlan Jolly; Associate Professor Quenten Schwarz; Professor Hamish Scott; Professor Paul Thomas; Doctor Kate Vandyke
Summary: The loss of a pregnancy or newborn is a devastating outcome for parents, with profound psychological, social and economic impacts. A lack of explanation for their loss is distressing for many parents and a lack of genomic diagnosis often means no options to reduce recurrence risk. Despite the Genomic Autopsy Study providing over 400 nationally referred couples with genomic testing, half of all families remain without a genetic cause; warranting further interrogation of the biological mechanisms.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Professor Vicki Clifton; Associate Professor Brian Cox; Doctor Arutha Kulasinghe; Professor Wendy Robinson; Doctor Sarah Elizabeth Steane
Summary: Often poor outcomes in pregnancy are attributed to very small babies but our Research shows babies of any size can die either in utero or after birth. We propose the risk of death of any sized baby is due to a poor functioning placenta. We will test this hypothesis by examining placentae from babies of all sizes that had an adverse outcome. This work will define the common placental mechanisms that lead to stillbirth and neonatal death regardless of the size of the baby at birth.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Doctor Antonia Shand; Ms Olga Aleshin; Doctor Diana Bond; Professor Clare Collins; Doctor Hartmut Cuny; Professor Sally Dunwoodie; Doctor Laura Gerhardy; Professor Natasha Nassar; Doctor Rachael Rodgers; Doctor Francisco Schneuer; Doctor Cansu Uzuner
Summary: This project will determine levels of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), a form of vitamin B3, and related metabolites among women with a history and/or experiencing miscarriage and compare with women without miscarriage. We will assess lived experience and determine role of diet, lifestyle, and number/timing of miscarriage. Findings will show links between NAD and miscarriage and identify potential biomarkers to predict future pregnancy loss, inform prevention, and target new treatments.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Doctor Wentao Li; Professor Georgina Chambers; Doctor Michael Costello; Doctor Oisin Fitzgerald; Associate Professor Tanya Nippita
Summary: This project aims to reduce pregnancy loss in assisted reproductive technology (ART), where around 20% of pregnancies are lost. Our goal is to understand the reasons for these losses and develop models to predict the risk of pregnancy loss. The findings and predictive tools for pregnancy loss in ART will be shared through a government-funded and trusted platform - YourIVFSuccess website. This will help couples and doctors make informed and personalised treatment decisions.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Professor Martha Hickey; Doctor Mridula Bandyopadhyay; Doctor Hsin-Fang Chung; Doctor Tessa Copp; Doctor Martina de Witte; Professor Jenny Doust; Professor Kirsten McCaffery; Professor Gita Mishra; Doctor Sally-Anne Mortlock; Associate Professor Michelle Peate; Doctor Sarah Price; Associate Professor Ines Rio
Summary: Around 10% of women experience early menopause (before age 45 years). This may follow surgery or cancer treatment, but is often spontaneous and in many cases the cause is not known. This will be the first study to determine the genetic and environmental risk factors for early menopause, deliver an evidence-based tool for diagnosis and management and new health information and support resources for culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) women who are at elevated risk of early menopause.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary:
Immunotherapy causes substantial damage to ovaries in mice. It is not known if immunotherapy can cause similar damage to human ovaries, leading to infertility and early-onset menopause. 
This is a crucial information gap for patients.  
This study will assess ovarian function in premenopausal women with early-stage, curable triple negative breast cancer receiving chemoimmunotherapy, and will provide the first prospective human data on the impact of chemoimmunotherapy on ovarian function.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Associate Professor Joanne Enticott; Mrs Susanne Baker; Professor Emily Callander; Mrs Kirsty Costa; Doctor Lan Du; Professor Megan Galbally; Doctor Alicia Jones; Ms Cailin Jordan; Doctor Samantha Kozica; Doctor Karen Magraith; Mr Yitayeh Mengistu; Associate Professor Lisa Moran; Doctor Sandra Reeder; Professor Helena Teede; Associate Professor Amanda Vincent
Summary: Around 16% of Australian women experience menopause before age 45, including those with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), which happens before 40. Early menopause can lead to health issues like infertility and dementia. Diagnosis is often delayed, causing distress and poorer health. We will develop a risk prediction tool for POI to enable early identification and better care. This will build on our work with international guidelines and the Ask Early Menopause App, helping women worldwide.

Summary: This project uses cutting-edge “multiomic” technologies to study patients with early menopause. We will validate likely genetic causes using innovative models of ovarian disease, including patient cells, in vitro assays and animal studies. We will also identify lifestyle and genetic risk factors for low ovarian reserve using a Western Australia birth cohort. Identifying cause enables personalised care, better outcomes, and pre-symptomatic diagnosis with opportunity for fertility preservation.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: The project aims to develop and evaluate an oral health assessment tool for non-dental professionals and carers who regularly interact with people with intellectual disability. Such a tool will allow early oral conditions to be detected, prevented from further progression, and promptly referred for treatment. It will effectively prevent oral diseases and allow vulnerable people with disability to live unaffected by oral pain and complications.

Summary: People with intellectual disability often have poor oral health. This can be from a lack of preventive oral health care, or from inadequate care from untrained disability support workers. This project will work with people with intellectual disability and disability services to co-create a cutting-edge online oral health education resource for disability support workers. The oral health of people with intellectual disability will be improved, with problems identified and treated earlier.

Summary: People with intellectual disabilities face poorer health outcomes, including higher rates of preventable deaths. Sometimes blood tests can be distressing, leading healthcare providers to skip essential tests. Blood tests are vital to manage health conditions, yet these are often overlooked. This project aims to test an idea that a team of healthcare professionals can look at several ways to complete a blood test, this might include gradually building up confidence, or sedating medications.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: The project aims to increase participation in physical activity for adults with intellectual disability who are more likely to be physically inactive than adults without disability. A cross-sector navigator program will be co-designed and delivered to provide support to adults with intellectual disability and their family to identify and participate in suitable physical activity. The program will be evaluated with likely outcomes of improved health and social benefits for people with disability.

Summary: People with severe and profound intellectual disabilities have complex health care needs and have difficulties accessing, managing, and deciding about their health care. When young people move to adult health care their needs are not always met. Profound Pathways is led by people with lived experience to highlight these urgent problems and to co-design solutions for health care transition and decision-making that better include people with severe and profound intellectual disabilities.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: This project will help young people with intellectual disability get better health care when they move from children's to adult health services. Working together with young people, families, doctors, advocates and educators, we will make tools and training to help people make their own health choices and get care that works for them. Led by people with disability, the project includes both First Nations and non-First Nations streams and will develop national guides to improve health services.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Professor Kate Laver; Doctor Manya Angley; Doctor Irene Belperi; Professor Gillian Caughey; Professor Maria Crotty; Doctor Kisani Manuel; Doctor Jacqueline Roseleur; Doctor Jessica Smith; Doctor Ruth Walker; Associate Professor Craig Whitehead
Summary: Australians aged 65+ can access aged health care, but this doesn't suit people with intellectual disabilities, who often age prematurely. Current policies create barriers to proper care. Inspired by Indigenous health policies, this project aims to set a fairer age for access and develop key health indicators. Researchers will analyse existing datasets, study ageing trends, and gather insights from affected communities to recommend better policies.

Summary:
This project will look at how health services in rural areas can be improved to better support older people with an intellectual disability. 

It has been co-designed with rural people with lived experience of intellectual disability. 

We will talk with people about their experiences with services. We will also look at how people's health changes over time. 

We will use this information to help services to work together to better support for older people with intellectual disability in rural areas.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: Routine health screening is a way to identify and address unmet needs to improve health outcomes among people with intellectual disability. Patient-reported outcome measures are a method of health screening in which patients can identify their own needs; the results can be used by health services to provide appropriate care. We will co-produce, implement and test a patient-reported outcome measure system for and with people with intellectual disability to improve their health outcomes.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research

Summary: People with intellectual disability often need support for their health. Sometimes their supports might miss signs that the person’s physical or mental health is changing. Our project will develop an AI tool to help notice these changes and seek medical help when needed. The tool will also help them talk about the signs with health professionals, so they can make health plans. We will work with people with intellectual disability and their supporters to co-design the AI tool and test it.

Summary: People with disability can experience difficulties navigating emergency departments, communicating their needs and preferences and understanding treatment options. Disability Liaison Officers (DLOs) act as a bridge between healthcare staff, patients and carers. Using a co-design framework, we will conduct a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial to assess the effect of DLOs on health outcomes and patient experience of people with intellectual and other developmental disabilities.

Summary: Pathogen genomics is a powerful new tool to understand infectious diseases transmission and outbreaks. The Australian Pathogen Genomics Program will embed pathogen genomic surveillance into practice nationally and optimise the surveillance approaches to reduce the burden of infectious diseases. The Program will also incorporate exciting new methods (such as wastewater surveillance) and ensure Australia's infectious diseases surveillance system is prepared for emerging threats.

Summary: Advances in genomics holds great promise to revolutionise our ability to treat patients with life-threatening infections. We will enrol more than 1200 ICU-admitted patients with suspected sepsis into a randomised trial, to compare a rapid host-biomarker test and targeted pathogen DNA sequencing from blood to guide antibiotic therapy. The trial will evaluate this novel approach, robustly assessing the clinical impact and health economic benefits in comparison to standard diagnostic methods.

Summary: We want to improve how we diagnose infections using cutting-edge technology. Instead of relying on traditional methods, we’ll use a more advanced approach that looks at all the genes of both the patient and the infection, specifically in areas like brain and lung infections. Our plan is to speed up diagnosis, find more accurate results, and create treatments tailored to each patient. This project will also reduce healthcare costs by helping doctors make more precise decisions.

Summary: Rapid precise genomics allows us to pinpoint the nature of AMR transmission in people and in hospitals and to identify how this spreads. We use rapidgenomics platforms to enable clinicians and public health officials to recognise AMR transmission and intervene in timely fashion. We will provide these tools in accessible reports that not only accelerate well-proven responses to disease transmission but also directly and immediately enable exciting new therapies that we have pioneered.

Summary: This project aims to use new technologies in healthcare, such as genome sequencing of bacteria that cause serious infections, combined with electronic medical record data from patients with these infections, to inform new diagnostics, optimised therapies and cutting-edge prevention of outbreaks of antimicrobial resistant organisms. New ways of analysis large amounts of data will be tested to help healthcare providers make the best decisions for patient care and hospital resource efficiencies.

Summary: Exotic mosquito-borne diseases like dengue, Zika, and Japanese encephalitis pose a growing threat to Australian communities. This project uses genomics and citizen science to predict mosquito vector invasions, detect mosquito-borne viruses, and empower communities. By predicting hotspots, creating detection tools, and involving schools, we aim to build a scalable early-warning system, improving public health preparedness to reduce arbovirus outbreak risks for safer Australian communities.

Summary: Over 700 medicines used in Australia show unpredictable effects, leading to safety issues and 275,000 hospitalizations annually. Better tools to predict how medicines will affect individuals could prevent 25% of these cases. Current methods focus on genetic testing, which hasn’t meaningfully changed in 40 years. This project explores a new approach: analyzing tiny liver particles found in blood to predict risks from non-genetic factors, improving medicine safety and reducing adverse events.

Summary: This project establishes a national network to improve children's cancer treatment using genetics. It has three parts: (1) Gathering data on treatment side effects and ensuring enrolment of diverse ancestry communities (2) linking genetic results to drug side effects and (3) improving the use of genotype informed prescribing by education for the workforce, web-portals of Research results and general public events. The goal is safer, more effective cancer treatment.

Summary: Building on their experience in the field of clinical pharmacogenomics (PGx) the investigators will identify and address the causes of the lack of clinical implementation by focusing on barriers including health records, molecular testing platforms and workforce education. We will demonstrate our impact in the fields of cancer therapy and organ transplant and use an Implementation Science approach to provide a general framework for accelerating the introduction of PGx into Australian hospitals.

Summary: This project aims to improve medication safety for Indigenous Australians by identifying genetic differences that affect how genes are expressed their interactions with medicines. Using advanced long-read sequencing and artificial intelligence, we will create a detailed map of important medicine-related genes. This Research will help develop equitable, scalable, and accurate pharmacogenomic guidelines to reduce harmful reactions and improve health outcomes for all.

Summary: Clopidogrel, used to prevent future heart attacks, is ineffective in a third of Australians. A gene test can identify these patients but isn’t done. This project aims to test all heart attack patients needing a stent in 5 NSW hospitals. Outcomes include identifying current antiplatelet prescribing, building practitioner/consumer knowledge, determining best testing methods, and assessing health and economic benefits. The goal is to ensure all Australians receive effective antiplatelet medicines.

Summary: This project will investigate whether existing pharmacogenetic tests can reduce medication harm from drugs used to treat mental health disorders in children and whether better tests can be developed.

Summary: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is common and diagnosed following several antidepressant trials-and-error rounds, resulting in significant adverse drug effects. Pharmacogenomics (PG), study of genetic factors impacting drug response, has improved antidepressant selection, however, 80% of people continue to experience depression following PG-guided treatment. We aim to conduct and integrate other genetic factors with PG, to improve prediction and precision treatment of TRD from the outset.

Summary: Every day, four Australian children are diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (T1D), a serious autoimmune condition, and often only after developing life-threatening complications. However, Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) could identify 80% of future cases early, before symptoms appear. This Research will explore if and how PRS can be used to detect T1D in Australian children, including the feasibility, acceptability and health system impact. The goal is to help shape a future national screening program.

Summary: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) are DNA tests that can identify individuals at high risk of Australia’s most common cancers (melanoma, breast, prostate and bowel). The ROSELLA trial aims to test how best we can deliver a PRS multi-cancer risk assessment to all Australians via general practice. If we can make risk assessment available to everyone equitably, we can ensure those most at risk of cancer receive the most appropriate cancer screening for their risk, reducing the burden of cancer for all.

Summary: Epilepsy is a common, complex neurological disease with both genetic and environmental risk factors. This project will explore whether certain metabolites are associated with epilepsy risk using genetic profiling. Our expectation is that some metabolic groups will be more important than others (e.g., lipids) and that this importance may be limited to or driven by certain epilepsy types. Patients can then be targeted for clinical interventions such as the addition of supplements to their diet.

Summary: Women can prevent breast and ovarian cancer if they know their personal risk and use risk-directed early detection and prevention strategies. This feasibility study will pilot an intervention involving a shared model of care between general practitioners and genetic counsellors to deliver a multifactorial breast and ovarian cancer risk assessment including polygenic information to young women. We will examine the intervention feasibility for deliverers, recipients, and the healthcare system.

Organisation: Council of the Queensland Institute of Medical Research

Summary: Despite the benefits of detecting cutaneous melanoma before it becomes metastatic, population-wide skin screening is not recommended as there is no evidence that it saves lives and can also lead to overdiagnosis of indolent lesions. We will undertake a randomised controlled trial to test if risk stratification based on a person’s genetic risk for melanoma improves adherence to recommended guidelines for skin screening while reducing unnecessary interventions and harms.

Summary: Mutations in BRCA1 mean that normal breast cells are less equipped to repairs themselves, driving breast cancer development. This has directed the way we screen and manage BRCA1 mutation carriers. In addition to rare mutations like BRCA1, small variations in 300 other genomic areas (polygenic risk score- PRS) can also elevate our breast cancer risk. We will determine how PRS is impacting the breast function to guide clinical management and the development of personalized preventatives.

Summary: Our goal is develop new genetic tests that can help reduce the number of people getting and dying from colorectal cancer.  Our hope is that these new tests will be able to be used by doctors to decide how to treat and monitor their colorectal cancer patients, and increase participation in colorectal cancer screening for older Australians, and can identify which younger Australians (who are currently too young for screening) are at high risk and could be offered screening.

Summary: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer impacting Australian men. Yet, distinguishing which men will receive a diagnosis remains a challenge. The key – our genetics. Using a multi-ethnic model and advanced pangenomic technologies, we will develop a new risk-prediction approach that interrogates for all variance across the human genome. The goal - a truly complete polygenic risk score to be used by clinicians to predict for prostate cancer risk and adversity, irrespective of patient ancestry.

Summary: Genomic testing has a critical role in treating rare inherited eye diseases (childhood glaucoma, congenital cataracts, and retinoblastoma). Yet, there is a gap in accessing genetics services identified by consumers. This project will explore barriers to accessing services through interviewing families and healthcare professionals, and subsequent workshops with key stakeholders will develop and trial solutions. Outcomes will be evidence-based recommendations trialled for effective implementation.

Summary: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a genetic condition that leads to extremely elevated cholesterol. It affects more than 100,000 Australians; yet more than 90% of people with this condition are unaware. People usually remain unaware of this genetic condition until they or a family member experience a heart attack. Our Research will enable family members of people with this condition to undergo genetic testing and manage their condition before it is too late.

Summary: The growing availability of genomic testing provides prospective parents with valuable insights into their future child's health. However, the benefits of such testing are unevenly distributed, as people from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds face many barriers to accessing genomic healthcare. The goal of this project is to build community trust and improve access to perinatal genomics for CALD communities through consumer-centred research.

Summary: Genomics promises better healthcare, but access is challenging. This project empowers nurses to facilitate access to genomics, using a practical compendium of resources co-created with nurses and consumers. We'll test this approach in cancer care, an area with many different testing needs, to help us refine and adapt the approach for other areas of health in the future. This could mean earlier diagnoses, more tailored treatments, and fairer access to the benefits of genomics.

Summary: Access to a genetic diagnosis and linked precise and supportive care is inequitable for people living in communities in regional and remote Australia, who are from culturally and linguistically diverse communities and who are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Our program is co-led by researchers from these priority communities and will explore how to overcome this inequity and test out a health solution, designed together with the communities, clinicians, health services and researchers.

Summary: To ensure genomic medicine can help everyone, we need data that fully represents our population. This project will make it easier for Australians from different cultures and diverse backgrounds to be part of genomics research. We will create and translate participant information, exploring new automated translation tools, and train researchers and bicultural workers to work with diverse communities to include them in genomics research. This will contribute to better health for all Australians.

Summary: During pregnancy, healthy microbes in the birth canal can protect against infections, but others can cause serious infections. Migrants from certain regions are more likely to carry drug-resistant microbes, and these harmful microbes can cause infection inside the womb putting lives of both mother and baby in danger. Our Research uses new technology to identify both beneficial and harmful microbes and their drug resistance from vaginal swabs. These tests will help us choose the right treatments.

Summary: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the biggest cause of death in Australia. South Asians have a higher CVD risk than individuals with European ancestry, but are under-represented in health and genomic Research that informs the development of Australian tools and guidelines for assessing CVD risk. This leads to inequity in access to appropriate healthcare. By addressing this data bias, this project will help develop more equitable strategies for preventing CVD in a diverse Australian population.

Summary: Cutting-edge genomics will be applied to prevent infectious diseases in culturally and linguistically diverse communities in Western Sydney, with a focus on the Pasifika diaspora. Experts in genomics and multicultural healthcare will work together to deliver a novel disease prevention and early treatment program. School-age children and their parents will participate in the study and test the ability of genomics to identify sources of infection and improve community health.

Summary: CONNECT-TBI will establish a national data asset to support the care and outcomes or people who experience moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (TBI).  Using an interdisciplinary and evidence-informed approach, CONNECT-TBI will gather data about all important aspects of a person’s traumatic brain injury (TBI), their treatment and care. The CONNECT-TBI data asset will be used to improve understanding of care and outcome pathways, and facilitate clinical trials and research.

Summary: Many people with mild traumatic brain injury have persistent symptoms. We  will evaluate a co-ordinated care model delivering psychological, physiotherapy and medical treatment for persistent post-concussional symptoms in adults of all ages, comparing outcomes of delivery in-person and via telehealth to facilitate treatment access for rural and remote communities. We will assess treatment delivery processes, costs and participant experience and evaluate a public hospital clinic.

Summary: Many people who sustain a concussion go on to experience debilitating persisting postconcussion symptoms (PPCS) for months to years after the injury. Effective interventions for PPCS are lacking; however, treatment with psilocybin (i.e., magic mushrooms) in other settings effectively alleviates a range of symptoms relevant to PPCS (e.g., headaches, cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety). Here we will conduct the first clinical trial investigating the efficacy of psilocybin therapy for PPCS.

Summary: Evidence-based practice can improve outcomes after a concussion, but 50% of people don’t get the care they need. The first Australian Concussion Clinical Practice Guidelines can improve patient outcomes but requires effective targeted implementation strategies. With consumers, we will bridge this gap in care by codesigning a patient-driven model of concussion care that integrates existing services through a novel Concussion Conversation Tool and an Australian Concussion Health Pathway.

Summary: The Social Brain Toolkit offers online programs to improve communication skills for people with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (TBI). A Virtual Clinic will be set up, which will include program delivery by student health professionals and mentoring by people with TBI. The project will compare the Virtual Clinic to usual care to see which is more effective. The aim is to create a sustainable model for TBI rehabilitation and strengthen the future health workforce.

Summary: Individuals with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury with pre-existing mental health difficulties such as depression and substance use are at greater risk of poor outcomes. Their management requires a well-coordinated and personalised mix of brain injury, mental health and drug and alcohol services. A best-practice model of care to support these individuals is currently unavailable. Our project aims to develop this model to facilitate more tailored and effective care and improve outcomes.

Summary: Child and youth concussion is a major community concern.  We have recently completed multiple linked Research studies that confirm our methods and interventions can i) assist families to safely manage their child's early recovery, accelerate return to normal activities. This application aims to now implement our work into clinical and community contexts, nationally, to minimise the long-term impacts of concussion.

Summary: This project will develop and test a supportive model of care for those who are impacted by a mild traumatic brain injury from domestic violence. This will be undertake through: (1) an expert consensus of what constitutes best practice care for this group; (2) co-designing a local model of care based on the expert consensus; and (3) testing the model of care with frontline domestic violence services. This work has the potential to alleviate the significant burden experienced by victim-survivors.

Summary: Utilising CUREator’s established and proven processes, in partnership with CSIRO, CUREator will identify and select 10-15 promising Australian biotechnology companies developing novel therapeutics for funding support. New and established SMEs will access competitive funding coupled with expert scientific and commercial guidance, international networks, hands-on support and mentorship to guide them through the critical development phases to the point of investment- or partnership-readiness. By aligning funding incentives and milestone-driven progress, CUREator will provide an important bridge to overcome the stop-start nature of translational Research and assist SMEs to secure follow-on funding and nurture the next generation of innovators.

Summary: ASPiRATION-2 Liquid will evaluate a novel approach to personalised therapy for advanced lung cancer using circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) testing through a patient’s journey to guide treatment. Plasma ctDNA analysis will be used to tailor treatment to the patient’s unique molecular profile, eliminating the need for invasive tissue biopsy. The first 5 years of the project will focus on patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose disease has progressed after first-line targeted therapy.

Summary: High-grade gliomas (HGG) affect >2,000 Australians annually and are the leading cause of death among young people. Most cases remain untreatable, with survival rates <15 months post-diagnosis. We demonstrated that combining the PKC inhibitor enzastaurin with the PI3K inhibitor paxalisib and radiation increased survival by 156% in HGG mouse models. Building on this, we developed JLD14, a novel PKC inhibitor with superior brain penetrance, potency, and selectivity. In this project, we will advance JLD14 through non/preclinical studies while developing additional PKC inhibitors as potential more favourable alternatives. Within 5 years, we aim to launch Phase I clinical trials in Australia, targeting TGA/FDA Phase II approvals within 10 years.

Summary: Endometriosis affects 11% of Australian women causing distressing symptoms such as pain and infertility. Several interventions are used to treat people with endometriosis but unfortunately, we do not know whether they actually work. None of them has been tested in high-quality randomised studies assessing effectiveness and their interactions remain unknown. Overall, the lack of randomised evidence assessing the effectiveness and long-term results of endometriosis treatments is leading to clinical uncertainty, variation in clinical care and treatment outcomes. We plan to design a large adaptive platform trial assessing multiple endometriosis treatments with the ultimate goal of improving outcomes for Australians living with endometriosis.

Summary: The PLATINUM inception project aims to address the critical lack of high-quality evidence in paediatric critical care by developing an adaptive platform trial (APT). Through extensive stakeholder engagement and guidance from international experts in innovative trial design, we will establish the PLATINUM Master Protocol and associated operational documentation. Led by a multidisciplinary team of senior researchers and EMCRs with the support of all ANZ Paediatric Intensive Care Units, we will leverage existing ANZ trial infrastructure and national data pipelines, integrated with consumer preferences, clinician insights, and robust statistical and health economic modelling to develop an APT ready for immediate submission to funding bodies.

Summary: Stroke remains a leading cause of disability. Recovery is driven by brain plasticity. Increasing plasticity could accelerate recovery and address intractable problems of persistent disability. This project will establish evidence and capability to demonstrate feasibility of upscaling to a national adaptive platform trial to evaluate therapies that can upregulate plasticity and accelerate stroke recovery. This project consists of two concurrent streams. Stream 1 will pilot our adaptive trial in South Australia, collecting data in a hub-satellite model, ensuring greater trial access across metropolitan and rural stroke hotspots. Stream 2 will develop required infrastructure and resources, and build onshore capacity, for upscaling nationally.

Summary: The iSEARCH Pre-Platform Pilot is urgently needed to show feasibility for a National Adaptive Platform Trial, modelled on the UK RECOVERY Trial, to assess if intrapartum use of (a) sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, (b) half-dose oxytocin and (c) future treatments prevent intrapartum hypoxia and its sequelae, especially in minority groups at greatest risk. We will initiate (1) relationships with community leaders and focus groups on stakeholder views on potential barriers, enablers and preferred outcome measures in a National Adaptive Platform Trial (2) endorsement from professional groups (3)  a trial website for randomisation and trial management and (4) a protocol with ethics approval for the National Adaptive Platform Trial.

Summary: PASSPORT is an adaptive platform trial that will address high-impact evidence gaps in sepsis care not amenable to traditional randomised controlled trials. PASSPORT will be conducted through the Paediatric Research in Emergency Departments International Collaborative and its established Research network. Consumers and priority groups will inform all aspects of the project.   Partnerships will ensure evidence is translated into  health service delivery through policy reform, maximising return on investment. This approach will accelerate the identification of effective therapies, improve health outcomes for critically ill Australian children with sepsis, and build Australian capacity to conduct adaptive platform trials.

Summary: The PODIUM (PlatfOrm for DIabetic Foot Ulcer Management) initiative is a Platform adaptive trial to test promising therapies in subjects with diabetic foot ulcers. Foot ulcers in diabetes is an area of major unmet need, and scarce investment. Best practice includes antibiotics, restoring blood supply, non-weight-bearing and wound dressings. Despite this, one in five ulcers fail to heal, catastrophically resulting in a limb amputation or fatality. This costs society over $1.6B annually in direct care costs and around 28,000 disability-adjusted life years lost. PODIUM will initially test 2 oral and 2 topical therapies in a rigorous trial to expedite discovery of the most effective treatments to increase healing and reduce adverse outcomes.

Summary: BEAT-CF is an established adaptive trial platform, with the purpose of patient-driven evidence, on, for and by people affected by cystic fibrosis (CF).  BEAT-CF has enrolled nearly a 1000 people with CF from CF centres across Australia. Amidst the transformation in CF management brought by modulator therapies, Research priorities have shifted toward minimising the burden and toxicity of CF-related treatment.  To this end, BEAT-CF MARS will nest a new domain to BEAT-CF’s existing platform to assess the safety of two antibiotic-sparing strategies for managing pulmonary exacerbations. The proposal addresses all of the scheme’s intended outcomes, 7 of MRFF’s 13 nominated Research priorities, and international consumer priorities for CF research

Summary: The Trial for Reducing Infection After Arthroplasty with Dilute povidone-iodine lavage (TRIAD) will examine if dilute intraoperative povidone-iodine lavage is superior in reducing surgical site infection (SSI) in hip and knee arthroplasty compared to saline lavage only. This study aims to generate robust, low-bias randomised clinical trial evidence that will significantly impact infection prevention clinical practices and healthcare policies in arthroplasty surgery.

Summary: Metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death and the prognosis for patients with metastatic NSCLC remains poor. Primary Radiotherapy In MEtastatic Lung cancer (PRIME-Lung) is a registry-based randomised controlled trial for 420 patients with metastatic NSCLC. It is designed as a pivotal phase III trial that will test whether eradication of the primary tumour through non-invasive radiotherapy will limit metastatic spread,  improve survival and quality of life in this critical area of unmet need. PRIME-Lung will use the highly successful national AURORA lung cancer registry with >5000 patients already enrolled, enabling cost-efficient phase III trial delivery and maximising external validity.

Summary: The Streamlining GlioblastoMA Radiation Therapy (SMART) trial is a nationwide registry-based Phase 3 randomised controlled trial embedded into the Brain Registry Australia: Innovation & TraNslation (BRAIN) that will address the unsatisfactorily high treatment burden for people affected by glioblastoma (GBM) – an aggressive brain cancer impacting all domains of life with a prognosis of less than 18 months. SMART will test if a shorter 4-week daily radiation therapy course, at a slightly higher dose per session, will result in non-inferior survival compared to the standard 6-week daily course, but improve the quality of life for patients and carers during a critical juncture in their lives, as well as benefit healthcare resourcing long-term.

Summary: Clinical trials have exploded worldwide to produce significant health benefits, but with high costs. Adaptive Platform Trials (APTs) offer a promising alternative, but their efficiency and cost effectiveness is unknown. We are a multidisciplinary team of health economists, statisticians, trialists and patients working to assess the efficiency and cost effectiveness of APTs versus conventional trials. Guided by End User and Patient Advisory Groups, we will conduct surveys, focus groups, Discrete Choice Experiments and modelling to quantify efficiency factors using our team’s existing APTs. We’ll extend our published trial efficiency model to produce an innovative ‘APT-Cost Effectiveness Simulation Tool’ designed and translated for end users.

Summary: The Better Evidence And Translation for Calciphylaxis (BEAT-Calci) trial is an Australian, international, adaptive platform trial focused on kidney disease research, specifically targeting calciphylaxis—a rare, devastating condition with painful ulcers and high mortality. This landmark platform was designed with accommodation of multi-domains to minimise barriers to participation in rare disease and shorten time to evidence generation. We will assess the effectiveness of the medium cut-off (MCO) dialyser vs conventional high flux dialyser in treating calciphylaxis. With industry support, a piloted intervention, and coordination with study sites, we seek funding to establish this domain with global leadership and recruitment in Australia.

Summary: Despite resulting in costs of $2 Billion per year, and having an enormous health, social, and domestic impact, The Lancet Neurology Commission on traumatic brain injury (TBI) identified Australia and New Zealand as having “no reliable data” concerning this devastating disease. The Australasian Traumatic Brain Injury Collaboration (ATBIC) will address this major knowledge and healthcare gap. More specifically, ATBIC will leverage the existing partnerships and data collection infrastructure of pre-hospital healthcare services and clinical quality registries (AROC, ANZICS CORE, ANZTR, Monash University), to establish a national dataset, that will offer insights into each phase of care provided to moderate-to-severe TBI (msTBI) patients.

Summary: Eating disorders (EDs) are complex and outcomes are poor. Yet due to a lack of routine clinical monitoring, we lack data that would otherwise support improvement and evaluation of policy and practice initiatives. We will deliver a project that will transform ED healthcare into a "learning health system". We will do this by co-designing with key stakeholders an innovative digital clinical quality registry that feeds back information on outcomes to clients, clinicians and government. We will then demonstrate the value of the registry to address unmet needs by using registry data to evaluate the ED Medicare scheme and build prediction models that will underpin a personalised approach to ED care, thereby innovating both policy and practice.

Summary:
We are transforming decision-making during pregnancy. We will create Australia’s first national perinatal data infrastructure; linking national birth data with maternal prescribing records and health outcomes for mothers & children. Our initiative aims to provide critical evidence on the safety of prescribed medications during pregnancy, revealing their effects.
Central to this effort is the SAFE Pregnancy platform—a user-friendly online tool co-designed with consumers. It will provide easy access to new evidence, supporting informed decision-making between pregnant women and their care teams. This infrastructure will continuously integrate new data and enhance the platform, promoting safer pregnancies and healthier families.

Summary: Australia has one of the highest asthma rates globally, significantly affecting children and First Nations People.  A cure remains elusive but is within grasp. Advances in biological profiling and data analysis offer new drug discovery opportunities, but progress has stalled due to a lack of data integration across studies. This prevents healthcare improvement and effective evaluation of new treatments.  The CURE Asthma Data Integration Research Engine (CURE-ADIRE) proposal, led by CI Dharmage, is  a flagship project of the CURE Asthma Initiative led by CI Anderson and aims to remove this barrier. It will unify Australian asthma cohorts in a national system, enhancing Research to discover and clinically test effective treatments and cures.

This collaboration with the Central Australian Aboriginal Congress builds on our 5-year project evaluating alcohol policies in the Northern Territory. The findings will inform policy makers and community with independent and timely information on the impacts of alcohol policy on alcohol consumption and harms for in Aboriginal peoples and in the general population.

Partnering with young people, governments and other services, we will provide evidence to shape alcohol policy and programs that are responsive to young people’s needs and effective in improving health and wellbeing.

Similarly, there has been a rapid escalation mental and physical ill-health amongst adolescents and young adults.  This project sets out to examine how these changes are linked to increasing levels of alcohol availability in the community, and the impact on health services and sectors. It does this through a 21 year retrospective study and  a new prospective study.

We will (1) survey youth as part of a 16-year longitudinal study, and (2) systematically review the existing evidence, to identify the impacts of increased alcohol access on youth physical and mental health. In collaboration with partners and consumers, results will inform prevention and harm minimisation approaches to reduce the burden of alcohol on young Australians.

Our team of consumers, medical experts and researchers will access young people at high drug use events and combine state-of-the-art social Research and drug identification technology to understand what they are actually taking, the  risks and impacts, and codesign effective responses to prevent and manage health harms.

Summary: First Nations Australians living in remote, regional and rural Australia have almost no access to clinical specialist treatment for alcohol dependence. Given evidence that telehealth increases access to treatment for First Nations Australians, is acceptable to them and improves their health, this project will support a First Nations led adaptation and evaluation of Clean Slate.

Effective substance use disorder interventions exist, but need modification for those with brain injury. This multistate project bridges the gap by co-designing a tailored interprofessional program for young people and evaluating its cost-effective implementation in existing services.

We will examine the impact of oral doses of THC, cannabidiol (CBD) and combination THC-CBD upon the outcomes of pain, mood, cravings, safety and consumer experience in people with both chronic back pain and opioid dependence, providing evidence to inform future trials.

A multidisciplinary approach underpinned by key preliminary data will address the large unmet medical need for a novel strong painkiller with minimal abuse/misuse liability to both alleviate and prevent moderate to severe pain in people with a current or past opioid use disorder (OUD). Results arising from this Research could greatly assist in curbing the opioid crisis.

The proposed study will use a mixed methods approach to codesign an optimal implementation strategy and assess the feasibility and acceptability of integrating an established online, clinician-assisted pain management program into alcohol and other drug residential services.

One key reason is that people in opioid agonist treatment are usually excluded form most pain management services. This creates a critical need for effective and accessible pain management programs that can be delivered in settings that minimise barriers to care. We will codesign a pain management program with consumers and health experts to address this gap.

Summary: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) is a rare chronic pain condition that occurs after a limb injury. Symptoms include severe pain, swelling, and sensitivity. Current treatments are ineffective, and Research suggests an autoimmune link. We propose testing new immunotherapies that boost regulatory T cells, which reduce inflammation and relieve pain, using a humanised mouse model of CRPS. This project will provide critical evidence for advancing to small-scale clinical trials in CRPS patients.

This type of pain is difficult to treat and most medicines come with side effects and don’t provide adequate relief in most cases. This project will focus on identifying new ways to treat pain and will develop new therapeutics that are safer and more effective.

We will partner with children and families to develop new and engaging ways to provide pain education for children with a range of abilities, to improve important outcomes for children and families.

Guideline recommended treatment of physiotherapy exercise has only small effects and does not take psychological distress into account. This trial will assess the feasibility of a optimised physiotherapist-led treatment that integrates physical and psychological care, and a new physiotherapist training model to deliver this care. It will pilot processes for a future large scale clinical trial that tests clinical and cost-effectiveness.

Summary: Our Grace Trial aims to investigate a new, novel treatment option for people living with Chronic Pelvic Pain (CPP). We will also test if poo transplants can improve some of the common symptoms of CPP including pain, as well as mental and physical health, to help people get back to their level of everyday functioning before they had CPP.

This study tests a new approach to support Indigenous peoples with chronic pain on their health care journey, and support clinicians to deliver culturally safe pain care. The findings will inform a larger study to improve outcomes for more Indigenous people with chronic pain.

Using antibiotics to clear the infection is a novel promising treatment for these people. Our study will establish the feasibility of conducting a trial to definitively establish the efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness of this promising new treatment.

overburdened public hospitals by managing thousands of patients each year with musculoskeletal conditions nonsurgically. We have recently designed a new model of care for the service to better match multidisciplinary care to patients’ needs, called MATCH. We will now test if service clinicians and patients think MATCH is feasible and acceptable for use in the service in a pilot trial.

The program will be tailored to Australia’s healthcare system, with input from doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and people with lived experience of chronic pain. A trial will assess its effectiveness, safety, and potential for reducing opioid-related harm in Australian primary care.

The Enhanced Paediatric in Primary Care (EPiPC) program has created local teams of GPs, paediatricians, and allied health professionals who deliver early treatment to improve the development, health and wellbeing of preschool rural children.

Our aim is to find the factors that culminate in different helpings to explain the diverse patient experience and common symptoms.

Our consumer-led initiative studies food and drink sensitivities in PASC patients to discover novel markers of disease. These markers will help develop diagnostic biosensors to improve understanding and treatment, enhancing the quality of life for affected individuals.

This work aims to better understand, diagnose, and treat PASC, which affects many Australians and often goes unrecognized by healthcare providers.

recover from the initial infection with SARS-CoV-2, causing ongoing health issues. Our research aims to find
specific markers in the blood and understand the underlying causes of these long-term symptoms. By identifying
these factors, our team hope to develop new diagnostics and treatments to improve the lives of those suffering from
PASC.

Here, we will investigate what changes metformin induces in Long COVID patients which will help us understand the causes of Long COVID.

This project aims at identifying their cellular sources, effects, and relevance to human disease. Using advanced mouse models and patient data, it aims to provide critical foundational knowledge to inform treatment strategies for maximal clinical benefit.

Summary: Some people experience prolonged symptoms after an infection, while others recover quickly. This variation is not fully understood due to the need for large sample sizes for robust predictions. Our consumer co-designed project will analyse predictors of post-infective fatigue using a large, pooled international sample and apply the results to the largest Australian Long COVID study. This will help understand who develops Long COVID and why, aiding doctors, patients, and policymakers.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Associate Professor Quan Huynh; Associate Professor Melinda Carrington; Associate Professor Verity Cleland; Ms Margaret Deerain; Professor David Dunstan; Associate Professor Erin Howden; Professor Ralph Maddison; Professor Thomas Marwick; Associate Professor Kerryn Pike; Professor Janette Radford; Doctor Andrew Ridge; Professor Paul Scuffham; Ms Susanne Tegen; Mrs Kristyn Whitmore
Summary: Long COVID can cause lasting health issues, including breathlessness and fatigue months after infection. We developed and tested a multidisciplinary intervention combining exercise and medical care and found it improved patients’ functional capacity. This research will work with patients and health experts to expand this program nationally using a risk-based, fully remote approach. Our goal is to reduce health burden, lower costs, and improve quality of life for those with Long COVID.

Summary: The BEACON model of care offers an innovative, service-based clinical pathway designed to bridge the gap between primary and specialist care through targeted education and peer-to-peer learning. It will also deliver scalable, evidence-based, and personalised treatments to people living with long COVID, helping them access the right care, closer to home. Its effectiveness will be tested in a national trial to ensure it truly improves care quality and health outcomes for those affected.

Scheme: MRFF Emerging Priorities and Consumer Driven Research
Investigators: Doctor Carolina Sandler; Professor Andrew Baillie; Professor Bernie Bissett; Associate Professor Erin Cvejic; Associate Professor Lucette Cysique; Professor Sarah Dennis; Doctor Jacqueline Epps; Professor Elizabeth Halcomb; Professor Rowena Ivers; Doctor Matthew Jones; Professor Andrew Lloyd; Doctor Carolyn Mazariego; Associate Professor Joel Rhee; Doctor Marie-Claire Seeley; Doctor Eng Joo Tan
Summary: People with Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) suffer with disabling symptoms like fatigue, brain fog and breathlessness. The SAGE trial will provide education and training to upskill GPs, practice nurses, allied health professionals, as well as patients, in the diagnosis and care of PASC. A new model of care will be tested comparing multidisciplinary symptom-focused rehabilitation (physical therapy and psychological support) compared to self-directed management in primary care.

Summary: This project aims to create a new model of care for culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities affected by post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC). The findings will help shape clinical guidelines and policy decisions, ensuring healthcare responses are fair and tailored to the varied needs of Australia's diverse population. By engaging communities directly, the project ensures that healthcare is inclusive, effective, and accessible for all.

Summary: Long COVID affects 3-10% of Australians, with a greater impact on Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) population who are less likely to access care. In this study, we will partner with CALD communities, cultural organisations, and primary care providers to develop a model that helps CALD patients recognise long COVID symptoms and supports doctors in managing these patients effectively. This will ensure accessible and equitable health outcomes for CALD Australians with long COVID.

Summary: Frail older people are more likely to experience long-term effects known as Post Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), which can harm their independence and quality of life. This project aims to test a flexible, effective model of care for these individuals. Partnering with aged care organisations, the study will assess its success and ensure it meets the needs of older people. By training the workforce and evaluating effectiveness and implementation, the project seeks to improve health outcomes.

Scheme: MRFF Preventive and Public Health Research

Summary: Our consumer co-designed prospective cohort study addresses the current problem of the delayed diagnosis of bronchiectasis in children, especially in Indigenous children living in remote communities. Through our multicentre cohort of 550 children, we will develop a diagnostic algorithm enriched with a blood marker to enhance accuracy. If successful, this approach could be transformative. Our study responds to identified consumer priorities and builds on current initiatives.

Summary: Low lung function in childhood is a significant predictor of chronic lung disease in adulthood. However, we currently lack sensitive lung function tests that be applied in young children. This project will provide the evidence needed to implement sensitive, easy-breathing lung function tests into the clinic. Early detection of lung function impairment will allow treatments to be offered in childhood to preserve lifelong lung health, reduce risk of chronic disease, and prevent premature death.

Scheme: MRFF Preventive and Public Health Research
